item.title: AWS Outlines Five-Step Framework for Managing Amazon Bedrock Costs via IAM Attribution
item.description:
AWS Outlines Five-Step Framework for Managing Amazon Bedrock Costs via IAM Attribution

Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between application development teams and those accountable for cloud spend. AWS has established a five-step framework to manage Amazon Bedrock costs, emphasizing invoice-grade attribution to specific identities and teams without the need for custom infrastructure.

🔍 Overview

Token consumption scales based on the degree of autonomy granted to a workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than the number of user interactions. Different application patterns result in distinct cost profiles:

  • Conversational Assistants: These typically issue one model invocation per user turn.
  • Agentic Workflows: Workflows such as AI coding assistants that plan changes and call tools issue many invocations per task and carry a larger context on each one.

🧩 The Five-Step Framework

Cost management follows a sequential process where each stage depends on the successful implementation of the ones before it. Teams that jump to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.

Stage Description Leadership
Attribute Ensures every dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. FinOps
Observe Logs every request with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Platform Engineering
Enforce Implements budgets with alerts and hard blocks where risk demands them. Platform Engineering
Optimize Uses platform defaults like model routing and caching to remove waste centrally. Platform Engineering
Operate Uses scorecards and review cadences to turn data into decisions. FinOps

⚙️ Key details

Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call across all models. This data appears in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0.

  • Identity Coverage: Attribution spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.
  • Shared Gateways: For LLM gateways using a single role, per-user visibility is restored by passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags via AWS STS.
  • Tagging and Analysis: Tags surface in CUR 2.0 with an iamPrincipal/ prefix and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation.
  • Inference Profiles: Application inference profiles are pre-created resources on the bedrock-runtime endpoint that carry cost allocation tags.

💡 Why it matters

Effective cost management requires moving beyond published averages, which are a poor substitute for actual workload numbers. By utilizing the AWS Pricing Calculator and CUR 2.0 data, organizations can measure what their workloads actually consume. The use of platform defaults—such as token limits and model routing—allows for central waste removal rather than requiring every individual team to manage efficiency manually.

#AmazonBedrock #FinOps #CloudSpend #GenerativeAI #AWS

Source: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Worldwide Express Deploys Multi-Agent AI for LTL Billing Exception Automation
item.description:
Worldwide Express Deploys Multi-Agent AI for LTL Billing Exception Automation

Worldwide Express, the $5 billion LTL freight arm of ShipStation Global, launched a multi‑agent AI solution built on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon EC2 that plugs into its SpeedShip transportation management system to automate billing exception handling.

🔍 Overview

  • Approximately $5 billion in system‑wide revenue, serving over 75 less‑than‑truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers.
  • Every month, $15 million in free cash flow was frozen in unresolved billing exceptions.
  • In LTL freight, roughly 14 % of invoices fail the standard three‑way match between purchase order, goods receipt, and carrier invoice.

🛠️ How it works

When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents. Each agent pulls the carrier’s billing rules and policies, makes a recommendation, and writes a plain‑language note into the same workflow analysts use.

Agent Primary Function
Invoice Matching Agent Finds the matching shipment record and flags line‑item mismatches (quantity or service code differences).
Pricing Variance Agent Compares the carrier’s charge to the contracted rate and determines whether a pricing difference is valid.
Accessorial Validation Agent Checks unexpected fees such as liftgate, residential surcharge, or reweigh adjustments against delivery events and carrier policy.

All three agents handle every carrier without carrier‑specific code; they simply retrieve each carrier’s tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds before deciding.

⚙️ Technical details

  • The solution is built on Amazon EC2 as the inference engine, with Amazon Bedrock providing AI reasoning.
  • Design emphasizes fine‑grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed.
  • Orchestration logic runs directly on EC2, keeping the AI workflow fully under the team’s control and allowing the use of open‑source agent libraries.
  • Agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs human analysts use, giving the AI exactly the same data view (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof).

📈 Results

  • 75 % reduction in active exceptions within six months of launch.
  • 4‑week improvement in time‑to‑cash.
  • $1 M annual savings from automation.
  • One‑time $10 M free cash‑flow infusion released from previously frozen funds.
  • The $15 M monthly frozen cash flow is now largely resolved.

💡 Why it matters

  • Billing exceptions in LTL freight require contextual judgment—interpreting carrier accessorial policies, comparing charges to shipment data, and validating amounts.
  • Automating the three most common dispute types (line‑item mismatches, pricing variances, unexpected accessorials) frees analysts to focus on higher‑value tasks.
  • The implementation shows how enterprise transportation management systems can be enhanced with controllable, multi‑agent AI while keeping decision logic in‑house.

#AI #Logistics #Automation #AWS

Source: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Kiro AI IDE and AWS Transform Enable Repeatable PHP‑to‑Java Migration
item.description:
Kiro AI IDE and AWS Transform Enable Repeatable PHP‑to‑Java Migration

A new AI‑enabled workflow lets teams move mature PHP applications to Java with a measurable, repeatable process.

🔍 Overview

  • “When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling.”
  • “Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi‑step engineering tasks with you in the loop.”
  • “AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large‑scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro.”

🧩 How it works

  • “The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight‑phase workflow.”
  • “This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it.”
  • “Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery).”
  • “The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects.”
  • “At the top is a global .kiro/ layer that every project draws on.”
  • “A shared, global layer under .kiro/ holds two Skills, php-model-discovery (the scanner) and php-to-java-migration (the eight‑phase playbook), plus the core‑workflow.md Steering file.”

⚙️ Key details

  • “Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step.”
  • “Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application.”
  • “Kiro then walks the eight‑phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins.”
  • “Use Kiro to work through the code first: run the skill on one application, read the generated Java, and run the tests.”
  • “When you want to migrate more, AWS Transform runs the same methodology agentically with review at the checkpoints the skill defines.”
  • “Kiro handles one application at a time and suits first‑of‑a‑kind frameworks.”
  • “AWS Transform runs many applications as parallel jobs.”
  • “Both paths read the same skill files, so every rulebook fix made in Kiro improves the next AWS Transform run, and vice versa.”
  • “The scanner is discover‑models.php, a single‑file, dependency‑free PHP command‑line tool that doesn’t execute the target code.”
  • “It only reads source text as tokens, so it runs against apps of your choice whether its dependencies are installed.”
  • “Each per‑project folder holds its own PHP source, Java output, and spec sub‑folder under .kiro/specs/, so improving the methodology once lets every project inherit the gain.”

🚀 Availability

  • “You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it.”
  • “Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application.”
  • “Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘fix the loop, not the code’ apply to an autonomous run.”

💡 Why it matters

  • Stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling are achieved by moving to Java.
  • An eight‑phase, parity‑first pipeline guarantees that the Java port matches the original PHP specification before it is accepted.
  • The same skill files power both an interactive, single‑application workflow (Kiro) and a large‑scale, parallel workflow (AWS Transform), ensuring consistency across projects.

#PHP #Java #AI #Migration #AWS

Source: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training
item.description:
AWS releases Ray Train Deep Learning Container for distributed PyTorch training

AWS has released the Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC), a pre-integrated software stack designed to simplify distributed machine learning training. The image is built, tested as a single unit, and maintained by AWS to ensure compatibility across the various libraries required for multi-node workloads.

🔍 Overview

The Ray Train DLC is a PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries layered on top. It includes the full HuggingFace training stack, allowing users to run fine-tuning jobs without building or pushing new images. AWS publishes these images to the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public, where they can be pulled without credentials.

Component Function
CUDA Runtime Provides the foundational environment for GPU acceleration.
PyTorch Compiled against the specific CUDA runtime in the image.
NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library for GPU communication.
EFA Libraries Userspace libraries for the Elastic Fabric Adapter.
AWS OFI NCCL Plugin Connects NCCL to EFA for high-performance networking.
Ray Coordinates the cluster and manages training libraries.

🧩 How it works

Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two distinct roles, both of which use the same tagged image. Whether running on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) via KubeRay or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), the container’s role is determined by the startup command.

  • Ray Head: Coordinates the cluster, tracks state in the global control store, and runs the dashboard and job server.
  • Ray Worker: Supplies GPUs and executes the training processes, connecting to the head’s address at startup.

On Kubernetes, the KubeRay operator adds a RayCluster resource that builds and maintains these groups from a single manifest.

⚙️ Key details

The Ray Train DLC is designed to be configured entirely from outside the image. Users specify instance types, GPU counts, and network transport settings through external configuration files rather than by modifying the container.

  • Compatibility: The image entrypoint automatically enables bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries if the host’s NVIDIA driver is older than the image’s CUDA version.
  • Performance: Collective operations between instances run over EFA automatically as soon as pods request it, as the EFA stack is pre-installed.
  • Testing: AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests.

🚀 Availability

The Ray Train DLC is available in the Amazon ECR repository under the train-ml tag prefix, sharing a repository with Ray Serve and Ray LLM DLCs.

A provided sample demonstrates the DLC’s capabilities by fine-tuning a Qwen2.5-1.5B model using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances.

#AWS #Ray #PyTorch #MachineLearning #Kubernetes

Source: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint for Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore
item.description:
Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint for Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore

This update details the architecture and reference implementation of an enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The platform is designed to manage the relationship between a central Platform team and domain-specific Workstream teams that build and own individual agents.

🔍 Overview

The platform operates on a multi-account model where the unit of scale is a Workstream cell rather than a manually configured agent. Enterprises can adopt this architecture through three primary operating models:

  • Centralized: A single AI/ML team builds and runs every agent.
  • Decentralized: Each business unit builds and operates its own agents.
  • Federated: A central Platform team provides shared, governed services while domain teams retain ownership of their agents, tools, and data.

🧩 How it works

The Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint is structured across four connected planes: developer experience, platform control, Workstream execution, and assurance and operations. It provides a repeatable per-Workstream deployment pattern that allows teams to ship and roll back independently within pre-approved boundaries.

Component Function
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Provides modular services including runtime, gateway, identity, memory, policy, registry, and evaluations.
Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint Adds enterprise contracts as deployable infrastructure as code, covering ownership, account boundaries, observability, and cost governance.
Inference Gateway Applies guardrails, restricts models and Regions, and enforces per-Workstream rate limits and token quotas.
MCP Gateway Authenticates tool discovery and invocation through the Model Context Protocol with least-privilege execution roles.
Evaluation Pipeline Gates each agent before promotion to production to ensure performance and safety.

⚙️ Key details

Workstream teams require a paved road that includes several technical requirements for secure operation:

  • Identity and Security: Short-lived workload identity and isolated runtime and memory for each agent.
  • Governance: Use of an approved inference gateway for all untrusted requests and authenticated tool targets with auditable owners.
  • Operational Control: Automated evaluation, telemetry, and the ability to restore previous agent runtime versions.
  • Resource Management: Teardown procedures that remove runtime, memory, and tool grants in dependency order to ensure no resources are left behind.

💡 Why it matters

This architecture addresses the specific needs of various enterprise stakeholders. Security and governance leads receive evidence of every workload call to models and tools, while FinOps teams can perform chargeback by team or business unit using AWS Cost Explorer. By enforcing per-Workstream budgets and quotas, the platform ensures that no single team can exhaust shared capacity. Additionally, agents are restricted to only approved models and subscribed tools, with unauthorized requests from other accounts or identities being automatically rejected.

#AmazonBedrock #AgentCore #AIPlatform #EnterpriseAI #AWS

Source: Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon SageMaker adds Seekable OCI indexing to lazy‑load deep learning container images
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker adds Seekable OCI indexing to lazy‑load deep learning container images

Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Processing jobs now support Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing, which removes the full container image download from the critical path and lets jobs start in seconds.

🔍 Overview

  • “Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits.”
  • “Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress.”
  • “For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job.”
  • “Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs, which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job.”

🧩 How it works

  • “With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy‑loads your container image.”
  • “It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes.”
  • “Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images.”
  • “Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately.”
  • “It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it.”
  • “A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image.”
  • “You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI‑compliant artifact linked to your original image.”
  • “Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid.”

📈 Measured results

  • “As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks.”
  • “SOCI‑indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance.”

⚙️ Adoption

  • “You adopt it by pointing to a pre‑indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image.”
  • “Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels.”
  • “When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly:”
  • “Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running.”
  • “You only gain faster startup.”
  • “You never risk breaking an existing workflow.”

💡 Why it matters

  • “The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure.”
  • “SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).”
  • “Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance.”
  • “It decompresses and writes every layer to disk.”
  • “For small images this takes seconds.”
  • “But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more.”
  • “That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time.”
  • “The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime.”
  • “We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI‑indexed lazy loading.”

#SageMaker #ContainerImages #SOCI #AWS #MLTraining

Source: Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage
item.description:
Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage

Exowatt has expanded its modular, dispatchable solar platform with AI agents that autonomously triage alarms and perform energy‑market analysis, using a serverless model‑customization pipeline on AWS.

🔍 Overview

  • Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems for energy‑intensive applications such as AI data centers.
  • The flagship Exowatt P3 captures solar energy with optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long‑duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand via a heat engine.
  • P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, avoiding multi‑year grid interconnection queues.
  • A fleet of AI agents monitors live alarms at the edge, where connectivity may be limited or absent.
  • The AI pipeline now turns raw operational data into a certified training set, a fine‑tuned model, and a deployed artifact in days rather than months.

🧩 How it works

Solar system

  • Optical lenses concentrate sunlight onto a thermal absorber.
  • Heat is stored in a thermal battery for long‑duration discharge.
  • A heat engine converts stored heat to electricity on demand.

AI pipeline

  • Raw alarm and market data are collected from each site.
  • Open‑weight base models are fine‑tuned with Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) on Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Serverless training allocates capacity on demand, allowing multiple experiments per day.
  • The best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry and hosted via Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import.
  • Edge‑deployed models run on no‑GPU controllers; cloud‑deployed models run in the Cloud EMS.

AWS services powering the pipeline

Service Role
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import Hosts the fine‑tuned Qwen3‑14B for Cloud EMS (private invocation)
Amazon Bedrock (Qwen3‑VL‑235B) Provides paraphrasing for alarm‑triage
Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.6) Provides paraphrasing for energy‑market analysis
Amazon SageMaker AI (serverless model customization) Fine‑tunes open‑weight base models using LoRA and SFT
Amazon SageMaker AI Model Registry Stores and versions the evaluated deployment artifact

⚙️ Key details

  • Edge alarm‑triage uses the Qwen3‑1.7B model, fine‑tuned for the specific hardware and logic of Exowatt’s EMS.
  • Cloud energy‑market analysis uses the larger Qwen3‑14B model.
  • The fine‑tuned models achieve higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost.
  • Models are small enough to run on edge controllers without GPUs yet accurate enough for autonomous operation.
  • The pipeline can be reused to build smaller, task‑specific models across the growing fleet of sites.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables data centers to come online quickly without waiting for grid interconnection.
  • Provides reliable alarm monitoring even when connectivity is intermittent.
  • Reduces operational cost by avoiding per‑decision calls to large frontier models.
  • Accelerates model development from months to days, supporting rapid deployment as the fleet scales toward thousands of units.

item.title: Updating MLOps Pipelines for Automated Edge Visual Inspection with SageMaker
item.description:
Updating MLOps Pipelines for Automated Edge Visual Inspection with SageMaker

An updated architecture pattern automates fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle management for visual quality inspection at the edge using the Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. The solution automates per-camera training, evaluation, compilation, and registration without requiring manual intervention, replacing the deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization.

🔍 Overview

When scaling visual inspection from a single proof-of-concept camera to dozens of plant lines with multiple cameras, a single computer vision model trained on pooled footage underperforms. Differences in camera angles, ambient light from bay doors, and glare off stainless surfaces require fine-tuned models for individual cameras. Managing thousands of models manually is impractical, creating the need for automated fleet-wide model lifecycle management.

This update builds on the pattern from the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge by updating to Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3 and integrating SageMaker Neo for edge model compilation.

🧩 How it works

Re-training requests arrive via an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. An AWS Lambda function initiates an AWS Step Functions execution per request, which acquires a slot via a DynamoDB semaphore to limit concurrent executions to at most five by default. This queuing mechanism drains request bursts steadily while keeping concurrent SageMaker training jobs within standard account quotas without needing a quota increase.

Each execution runs a 13-step, dual-branch SageMaker Pipeline parameterized by camera ID:

  • Parallel Entry Steps: Three entry steps execute in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. Warm-start steps filter by camera ID metadata to resume training from that camera’s specific history.
  • Dual-Branch Training: One branch trains a small convolutional autoencoder that learns normal product appearance and flags anomalies using reconstruction error. The second branch fine-tunes a ResNet18 classifier to confirm defects.
  • Evaluation and Quality Gates: Both branches export trained models to ONNX and evaluate them against held-out data. Quality gates block underperforming models from proceeding.
  • Compilation and Registration: Models passing the quality gate are compiled with SageMaker Neo for the specific edge target and registered in the SageMaker Model Registry as device-ready artifacts.
  • Notifications: Pipeline completions publish to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Operational failures are routed to the same topic via Amazon EventBridge, preserving the original error details.

⚙️ Key details

Pipeline Component Function
Amazon SQS FIFO Queue Queues re-training requests
AWS Lambda & Step Functions Orchestrates pipeline execution flow
DynamoDB Semaphore Restricts concurrency to 5 active jobs to fit standard quotas
Convolutional Autoencoder Learns normal product traits and detects anomalies via reconstruction error
ResNet18 Classifier Fine-tuned model that confirms defects
Amazon SageMaker Neo Compiles ONNX artifacts for specified edge device targets
SageMaker Model Registry Stores versioned, device-optimized model packages
Amazon SNS & EventBridge Handles success notifications and operational failure alerts

💡 Cost and deployment

The entire solution is deployed using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). Note that older CLI versions fail due to a cloud assembly schema mismatch with recent aws-cdk-lib versions. Running a full pipeline execution on synthetic data costs approximately $0.07 in compute, and the complete sample code is published in the aws-samples GitHub repository.

#AWS #SageMaker #MLOps #ComputerVision #EdgeComputing

Source: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3 | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI Introduces Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Agents
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI Introduces Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Agents

Amazon SageMaker AI has introduced Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL), a serverless capability designed to train models on sequences of actions where the only reliable feedback is whether the entire sequence succeeded.

💡 Why it matters

Most fine-tuning focuses on producing a better answer to a single prompt. However, agents performing tasks like triaging support tickets or filing expense reports require a sequence of actions where each step depends on previous outcomes. Traditional supervised fine-tuning lacks labels for these sequences, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit decisions made several steps before an outcome.

🧩 How it works

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning trains models using the following architecture and process:

  • Infrastructure: SageMaker AI owns the training job and policy model. It sends prompts through an AWS Lambda forwarder to an agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or other infrastructure such as Amazon EKS, Amazon EC2, or AWS Fargate.
  • Execution: The agent calls the policy model, acts in the environment for as many turns as needed, and reports a single reward at the end of the episode.
  • Optimization: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) updates a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter on the policy model based on the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word.
  • Deployment: A single Python file deployed to AgentCore contains the environment, the tool, and the scoring function.

⚙️ Key details

To demonstrate MTRL, a run was conducted using the game Wordle and the GPT-OSS-20B model. Wordle was selected because its rules are few, guesses depend on previous feedback, and outcomes are scored objectively.

item.title: TorchNeuron Model Support Space Shows Which Transformers Run on AWS Trainium
item.description:
TorchNeuron Model Support Space Shows Which Transformers Run on AWS Trainium

🔍 Overview

A new Hugging Face Space, torch‑neuronx‑model‑support, lets you see whether a given Transformers model runs unmodified on AWS Trainium and provides the exact script to run it yourself.

🛠️ How it works

  • Uses the torch‑neuronx package, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium.
  • Runs Transformers models on Trainium the same way they run on any other device.
  • The provided run.py script loads the model with from_pretrained, shards it when needed, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

📊 What the Space displays

  • PASS/FAIL result for each model.
  • Number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over.
  • Wall‑time of the run (compilation included).
  • Peak device memory usage.
  • The Neuron stack version, required packages, and the run.py script used.
  • If a model is omitted, the Space explains why (e.g., not prioritized or truly incompatible).

📈 Testing methodology

  • Tests run on a Trainium2 (trn2) instance, typically in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container.
  • Each model is sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights (maximum 16 cores, i.e., four Trainium2 devices).
  • Most models use tensor parallelism; Mixture‑of‑Experts models without a tensor‑parallel plan use expert parallelism only.
  • The test generates 32 tokens and checks them.
    • On a single core, the tokens are compared with a CPU run of the same checkpoint.
    • When sharded, a small judge model verifies that the text is fluent English.
  • A PASS only confirms correctness of the 32‑token output; it says nothing about throughput or longer generations.

⚙️ Configurability

  • The Space opens on the Selected view (our own selection of top‑downloaded and trending models).
  • You can switch to Trending or Downloads views and type part of a model name to look it up.
  • Versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx‑cc) and Transformers library can be chosen.
  • When a model is left out on purpose, the Space tells you the reason.

📌 Current scope

  • Only Transformers models are tested.
  • The selection is limited to text‑generation and image‑text‑to‑text models.
  • Only models that fit on four Trainium2 devices (up to 16 cores) are included.

🚀 Getting started

  1. Open the Space (it starts on the Selected view).
  2. Choose the desired neuronx‑cc and Transformers versions.
  3. Follow the displayed run.py script: install the listed packages, then run on a trn2 instance.
  4. The first run compiles the model’s graphs; subsequent runs can reuse compiled graphs by copying them from the public NEFF cache bucket.

🔎 Where the data comes from

  • All rows are sourced from the public aws‑neuron/torch‑neuronx‑model‑support dataset.
  • The dataset contains one Parquet file per pair of neuronx‑cc and library versions.
  • Each row stores the model’s result, any error, the stack versions, and the run.py script that was executed.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

item.title: Open Responses API becomes vendor‑neutral standard with AWS Bedrock support
item.description:
Open Responses API becomes vendor‑neutral standard with AWS Bedrock support

The Open Responses open‑source specification has moved into a vendor‑neutral home under the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) and is now implemented at scale by Amazon Bedrock, giving developers a single API format for calling language models, streaming results, and orchestrating tool use.

🔍 Overview

  • The API format that a growing number of model providers use to call language models now has a vendor‑neutral home.\
  • Open Responses joined the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) as a project, bringing it under open governance alongside MCP and A2A.\
  • Open Responses is an open source specification that defines a single API format for calling language models, streaming results, and orchestrating tool use.\
  • AWS is involved in Open Responses and employs a core maintainer on the project; Amazon Bedrock already supports the Responses API across dozens of models.

🧩 How it works

  • Common request/response model – one schema for structured inputs and outputs that works across OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, local models, and any provider that implements the spec.\
  • Agentic loop – a unified pattern for models to emit tool calls, receive results, and continue reasoning, whether tools are developer‑hosted or provider‑hosted.\
  • Items as the atomic unit of context – a clear schema for messages, tool invocations, and reasoning state, with defined state machines (in_progress, completed, failed) for predictable behavior.\
  • Semantic streaming events – meaningful event types like response.output_text.delta and response.completed rather than raw text deltas, so clients can be built once and work across providers.\
  • Extensibility without fragmentation – provider‑specific tools and item types are namespaced with provider slugs, keeping the portable core clean while preserving room for innovation.

⚙️ Key details

  • OpenAI pioneered the Responses API for stateful conversations that call external tools or functions.\
  • Anthropic’s Messages API and Google’s Gemini API use different conventions; Open Responses standardizes these concepts with versioning, compliance tests, and extensibility rules.\
  • AWS is a member of the AAIF Governing Board and contributes to Open Responses’ development as an AAIF project.\
  • By housing Open Responses under AAIF alongside MCP and A2A, the specification evolves through community consensus, not any single company’s product roadmap.\
  • Bedrock’s implementation provides a production‑grade reference for how the spec works at scale.

🚀 Availability

  • Amazon Bedrock has supported the Responses API since December 2025 and continues to expand its implementation.\
  • Developers can use the familiar OpenAI SDK to call models hosted on Bedrock simply by changing the base URL and API key.\
  • Bedrock’s Responses API support includes:
    • Stateful conversation management via previous_response_id (no need to pass the full conversation history with each request).
    • Built‑in tool use for agentic workflows, including developer‑hosted and server‑side custom tools (server‑side tool support added in January 2026).
    • Streaming and non‑streaming modes across both bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints.
    • Broad model availability – the Responses API works with models from Amazon, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Google, and others, all through the same API format.
  • Existing applications built against the OpenAI Responses API can run on Bedrock with minimal changes, gaining access to Bedrock’s features such as Guardrails, cross‑Region inference, and intelligent prompt routing while keeping the same client code.
  • Recent additions include WebSocket transport for persistent connections and a compaction endpoint for managing long conversation contexts.

💡 Why it matters

  • For developers – one schema and compliance tests mean integration code can be written once and reused across providers.\
  • For model providers and inference platforms – Open Responses gives a clear specification to implement, avoiding the need to learn multiple proprietary APIs.\
  • Community governance – the AAIF framework ensures the spec evolves through consensus, fostering interoperability across the rapidly expanding landscape of language‑model providers.

Source: Open Responses Joins AAIF with AWS Support | Amazon Web Services

item.title: i14 Ports Laplace 3B Linear Attention Model to AWS Trainium2
item.description:
i14 Ports Laplace 3B Linear Attention Model to AWS Trainium2

AI research company i14 has updated the implementation of Laplace 3B, a linear attention alternative to traditional transformer architectures, by bringing the model to AWS Trainium2 using TorchNeuron Native.

💡 Why it matters

Most large language models (LLMs) utilize transformer architectures with softmax attention, which causes the key-value (KV) cache to grow as conversation or document context increases. This growth can lead to:

  • Reduced concurrency
  • Increased serving costs
  • The need for agentic applications to discard useful history

🧩 How it works

Laplace 3B is a 24-layer decoder that replaces softmax attention with Simple Gated Linear Attention (GLA).

  • Linear Attention: Reorganizes computation around a recurrent state updated for each token, changing training attention complexity from O(T2) to O(T).
  • Context Compression: GLA compresses prior context into a fixed-size matrix state.
  • Fixed State: The inference state remains fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length.

⚙️ Key details

Working with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC), i14 transitioned the model from GPU-optimized Triton kernels to the TorchNeuron Native PyTorch backend. Technical adjustments included:

  • Kernel Optimization: The team replaced the fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer.
  • Compiler Compatibility: The 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence were statically unrolled to fit the on-chip memory limits and graph-size of the compiler.
  • Throughput Improvements: Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 increased throughput by 1.63 times and reduced per-rank traffic by 24 times.

Hardware Specifications

Laplace 3B was deployed on a trn2.48xlarge instance, which features:

Component Specification
Chips 16 Trainium2 chips
NeuronCores 64 logical NeuronCores
Connectivity NeuronLink-v3
SBUF 28 MiB State Buffer with 128 partitions per NeuronCore
PSUM 2 MiB partial-sum buffer wired to a 128×128 systolic Tensor Engine

Performance Metrics

On one trn2.48xlarge instance, the model achieved the following:

  • Training Speed: Approximately 120,000 tokens per second.
  • Inference Throughput: 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences.

item.title: Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS
item.description:
Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS

Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations, but MCP has no built-in authentication standard. This post shows how to fill that gap using Keyfactor EJBCA together with AWS services.

🔍 Overview

  • Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources.
  • MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations.
  • MCP has no built‑in authentication standard.

🛠️ Architecture

The solution combines Keyfactor EJBCA with several AWS managed services and implements three authentication layers that protect each trust boundary in the agent communication chain.

AWS Service Role in the architecture
Amazon Bedrock (via Strands Agents SDK) LLM inference for agents
Amazon RDS for MySQL Application database accessed through MCP tools
Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) Email delivery for the Email Agent
AWS Secrets Manager Secure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata
Amazon EC2 Hosts Keycloak identity provider and EJBCA PKI server

🔐 Authentication Layers

  1. Layer 1 – User Auth (User → System)
    • Uses OAuth together with an X.509 certificate and delegation minting.
    • Provides user identity and credential binding.
  2. Layer 2 – Agent‑to‑Agent (Agent → Agent)
    • Relies on signed request envelopes containing proof‑of‑possession, a nonce, and a timestamp.
    • Guarantees caller identity, request freshness, and prevents replay.
  3. Layer 3 – MCP Auth (Agent → Tool Server)
    • Combines a scoped token, the signed envelope, and a delegation assertion.
    • Covers all identities, creates a full authorization chain, and incorporates OCSP validation.

⚙️ Key Components & Controls

item.title: AWS Agent Registry enables runtime tool discovery for enterprise AI agents
item.description:
AWS Agent Registry enables runtime tool discovery for enterprise AI agents

AWS Agent Registry is a managed service designed for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills to address the limitations of hardcoded tool integration in enterprise systems.

💡 Why it matters

In enterprise SaaS engagements, systems often expose hundreds of internal APIs for customer data, inventory, orders, support, and pricing. Relying on build-time wiring for these tools can create several bottlenecks:

  • Scalability: Hardcoded tools function well for a few, degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that.
  • Performance: Models may spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about user requests.
  • Operational Overhead: Each new capability typically requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and coordinated releases across teams.

🧩 How it works

Instead of compiling every tool into the agent, an orchestrator can discover relevant tools at runtime:

  1. Registration: Publishers register searchable descriptions and protocol-specific descriptors.
  2. Search: The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane.
  3. Response: The registry returns record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors (such as an A2A agent card or MCP server metadata).
  4. Client Construction: The orchestrator constructs a client for each returned record based on the descriptor type.
  5. Execution: An ephemeral inner agent is built using only the dynamically discovered tools. The LLM selects the appropriate tool, synthesizes the result for the user, and the inner agent and clients are torn down after the turn.

⚙️ Key details

To maintain security, registry search results do not return authentication schemes or invocation credentials. The application must apply credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path.

item.title: Bi-directional KV Cache Transfer Cuts Latency for Multi-turn AI Agents
item.description:
Bi-directional KV Cache Transfer Cuts Latency for Multi-turn AI Agents

Multi‑turn agentic workloads accumulate context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. Each new turn resends the full conversation history – system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses – causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly.

🔍 Overview

  • In Prefill‑decode (P‑D) disaggregation, a prefill node builds the key‑value (KV) cache for the prompt, while a decode node retrieves those KV blocks to generate the response.
  • Conventional disaggregated serving moves KV cache only from prefill → decode. This one‑directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi‑turn workloads:
    1. After a response, the decode node holds KV entries for both the prompt and newly generated tokens. The prefill node cannot retrieve these entries for the next turn and must recompute KV projections for the previous response tokens.
    2. Session state is kept on the decode node but not on prefill nodes, increasing the chance of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill side.
  • When a full cache miss occurs, the prefill node recomputes KV projections for the entire conversation history, consuming more accelerator capacity and increasing time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT).

#AIInference #KVCache #MultiTurnAgents #AWS

Serving efficiency determines the amount of audio Deepgram can process within a specific infrastructure budget. By utilizing AWS AI chips, Deepgram achieved the following:

item.title: Push‑based NIXL connector speeds up vLLM inference on AWS EFA
item.description:
Push‑based NIXL connector speeds up vLLM inference on AWS EFA

vLLM’s new push‑based NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector reduces transfer latency between prefill and decode stages, delivering up to 3× faster first‑token latency and 30 % lower time‑per‑output‑token on AWS instances.

🔍 Overview

  • vLLM is an open‑source inference and serving engine for large language models.
  • It separates prefill and decode into separate engine instances (prefill‑decode disaggregation) so each phase can scale and be optimized independently.
  • KV‑block data moves between instances via the NIXL connector, which exploits RDMA‑capable interconnects such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).
  • The default NIXL mode is pull‑based; the new push‑based mode moves coordination off the critical path.

🧩 How the push‑based connector works

  • Three actors are coordinated:
    1. Decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the prefill instance is still computing KV.
    2. Prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer.
    3. A background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward‑pass loop.
  • Registration (identity + block locations) is sent as an NIXL notification during the same engine step.
  • Transfer starts when the later of two events occurs (registration arrival or prefill completion).
  • Requests are paired by ID; the matching logic handles reissued, preempted, or retried requests.
  • Once matched, the producer opens a connection (if needed) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each tensor‑parallel rank.
  • Producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts; each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes.
  • Each WRITE includes a completion notification.

⚙️ Key technical details

  • NIXL moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), avoiding host‑memory staging.
  • On supported instance types, AWS EFA provides GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA.
  • The push mode removes the serialization inherent in the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work.
  • Transfer‑setup time runs on the prefill side and on a background thread, not on the decode instance.

🚀 Performance

Mode TTFT improvement TPOT improvement
Pull (default) baseline baseline
Push (new) up to 3× faster up to 30 % faster
  • Benchmarks were run on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA.
  • Model: Qwen3‑32B.
  • The same push‑mode gains were observed on AWS Trainium clusters and on GPU clusters, confirming accelerator‑agnostic benefits.

💡 Why it matters

  • Direct KV block transfer between device memories reduces latency and improves throughput for large language model serving.
  • Overlapping coordination with computation maximizes utilization of high‑performance interconnects such as EFA.
  • The feature is contributed back to the open‑source vLLM project, making it available to any deployment that can use RDMA‑capable networking.

#vLLM #NIXL #AWS

Source: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM | Amazon Web Services

    • Traces each failure back to its root cause—data, prompt, or agent code.

item.title: AWS Introduces Trust in Depth Framework for Safer AI Agents
item.description:
AWS Introduces Trust in Depth Framework for Safer AI Agents

AWS is extending its long‑standing Defense‑in‑Depth discipline to AI agents with a new “Trust in Depth” framework.

🔍 Overview

  • Agents can take different execution paths each time they run. (“Run the same task twice and it might take a different route each time.”)
  • Traditional safety relies on a human in the loop approving everything the agent does. (“The usual answer is a person in the loop, approving everything the agent does.”)
  • That approach works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in. (“That works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in.”)
  • People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter. (“People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter.”)
  • Caution becomes a bottleneck, leaving capable agents idle on valuable work. (“Caution becomes a bottleneck, and agents capable of far more sit idle on the valuable work that could be making more of an impact.”)

🛡️ Trust in Depth Concept

  • AWS calls the new layered discipline “Trust in Depth.” (“AWS calls it Trust in Depth.”)
  • It repurposes the industry’s two‑decade‑old Defense in Depth model, which limits what can go wrong, to expand what can be safely allowed. (“Trust comes from independent layers that reinforce one another, the same layered discipline the industry has practiced for two decades as Defense in Depth, turned to a new purpose. Where Defense in Depth limits what can go wrong, this expands what you can safely allow.”)
  • The framework consists of four stages:
    • Scope – define the agent’s purpose, required capabilities, and absolute prohibitions before it runs. (“Scope, before it runs: What is this agent for, what capabilities does the job require, and what must it never do?”)
    • Know – record who authorized the agent, its identity, and ensure every acting agent is accounted for at deployment. (“Know, at deployment: Who authorized it, what identity does it carry, and can you account for every agent acting on your behalf?”)
    • Bound – enforce that actions stay within set limits while the agent runs and verify it can still do the job. (“Bound, while it runs: Do its actions stay within the limits you set, and can it still do the job?”)
    • Observe – reconstruct the agent’s behavior after each run to enable learning. (“Observe, after each run: Can you reconstruct what the agent did and why, and learn from it?”)

🤖 Automated Reasoning

  • Automated reasoning is mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. (“The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case.”)
  • It can produce a proof that a rule holds on every path described by a precise system model, or pinpoint the exact case where it fails. (“It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof.”)
  • The proof is only as good as the underlying rules and assumptions, making the design work before deployment the hardest part. (“It is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs.”)
  • AWS has used automated reasoning in production for over a decade on services such as IAM (handling more than 2.1 billion requests per second), the Nitro Hypervisor, S3 Block Public Access, and the VPC Reachability Analyzer. (“AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents.”)

🛠️ Kiro – Building Agents with Rigor

  • Kiro is an agentic coding system that applies structured, spec‑driven requirements before any code is written. (“Kiro, the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high‑level intent into structured, spec‑driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written.”)
  • When a rule can be proven, the agent may act autonomously; when proof does not apply, the framework limits the agent’s access and escalates ambiguous cases to a human. (“Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment.”)

💡 Why It Matters

  • As agents handle higher‑stakes work such as financial transactions, a single mistake can be increasingly harmful. (“As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful.”)
  • Organizations need confidence that an AI agent will stay within defined limits even when no one is watching. (“Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching.”)
  • Traditional safeguards—content filtering, testing, and monitoring—are each necessary but none alone can guarantee correct future behavior. (“Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs.”)
  • By combining scoped intent, identity tracking, runtime bounds, post‑run observation, and automated reasoning, Trust in Depth provides a repeatable, auditable safety net for AI agents.

#AWS #AIAgents #AutomatedReasoning #TrustInDepth

Source: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS launches Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments for AI agent transaction automation
item.description:
AWS launches Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments for AI agent transaction automation

When an AI agent accesses a paid resource, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. AWS now offers a managed way for agents to handle that payment automatically.

🔍 Overview

  • Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine‑to‑machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent.
  • The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP‑based machine‑to‑machine payments.
  • Integrated with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments, the service discovers, accesses, and pays for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously.

🧩 How it works

  1. An agent running in Anchor Browser makes a request (e.g., fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data‑enrichment API).
  2. The server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required together with the amount, accepted payment methods, and a payment address.
  3. AgentCore payments detects and parses the 402 challenge, distinguishes it from other 4xx errors, and constructs the correct payment header with the required cryptographic proof.
  4. The payment is processed through the x402 protocol; the original request is resubmitted with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context.
  5. The transaction is authorized and completed within the agent’s configured budget, and observability data (attempts, approvals, denials, settlements) is sent to Amazon CloudWatch.

⚙️ Key details

Component Role
Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments Cloud‑based browser automation purpose‑built for AI agents; manages authentication, navigation, network capture, and live view
x402 protocol Open standard for HTTP‑based machine‑to‑machine payments
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments Fully managed capability that manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits, processes x402 payments, and provides audit logs

Additional capabilities

  • Supports multiple payment schemes (exact, up‑to, and protocol variants) without hard‑coding vendor logic.
  • Maintains compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that may differ in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing.
  • Stores a private key for signing payments, with secure key storage, key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover.
  • Enforces per‑session and per‑transaction spend limits with real‑time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions.
  • Captures every payment attempt, approval, denial, and settlement in audit logs for compliance and reconciliation.
  • Provides idempotency, essential for wallet operations.

🚀 Availability

  • Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory.
  • The solution is now available on AWS Marketplace.

💡 Why it matters

  • Without a managed payment service, an agent would need to internalize the entire payment stack, including secure key management and budget enforcement.
  • Browser‑based agents have the additional constraint that payment must occur within the same browser session; the integrated service satisfies this requirement automatically.
  • Built‑in observability and spending limits help operators maintain control and compliance while allowing AI agents to autonomously access paid APIs and content.

item.title: Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
item.description:
Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers

This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the multi‑node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers. The deployment separates the prefill and decode phases onto distinct GPU workers behind a single OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.

🔍 Overview

  • Ray is a distributed compute framework; Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes.
  • AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) are pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately.
  • The new Ray LLM DLC extends this approach to multi‑node inference.

🏗️ Architecture

  • CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod (CPU‑only).
  • Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run Ray workers: one dedicated to the prefill phase, the other to the decode phase.
  • Both GPU nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
  • KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and automatically wires the head‑to‑worker join.
  • Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers.
  • KV‑cache generated by prefill is transferred to the decode worker over NIXL, using the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) through NIXL’s libfabric backend.

⚙️ How It Works

  • Prefill phase
    • Processes the entire input prompt in parallel.
    • Builds the key‑value (KV) cache.
    • Compute‑bound.
  • Decode phase
    • Generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending the KV cache.
    • Memory‑bandwidth‑bound.
  • Separating the phases prevents compute‑heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress.
  • Disaggregation allows each phase to use hardware and serving properties tuned to its workload, improving overall performance at scale.
  • The trade‑off is that the KV cache must be handed from prefill to decode quickly enough to retain the benefit.

📦 Key Components

Component Role
Ray LLM DLC Packages Ray Serve LLM, NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL), and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack; exposes an OpenAI‑compatible API with no application code
vLLM Inference engine
Ray Serve HTTP Serving layer
NIXL KV‑cache transfer between nodes
EFA stack (libfabric, aws‑ofi‑nccl) High‑bandwidth node‑to‑node communication
AWS Deep Learning Containers Pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images ensuring no version drift between CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer

🚀 Deployment Details

  • The Ray LLM DLC ships Ray Serve LLM, NIXL, and the EFA stack, ready for multi‑node inference.
  • No application code is required to expose the OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.
  • This multi‑node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as for prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads.
  • In a previous post, the Ray Serve DLC was used to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By assigning prefill and decode to separate GPUs, compute‑heavy prefill work no longer contends with latency‑sensitive decode work.
  • Independent scaling of each phase enables better resource utilization and lower latency for LLM serving at scale.
  • All components are validated together before each release, guaranteeing compatibility across the CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer.

  • AWS IAM Identity Center provides centralized authentication and federates with external providers such as Microsoft Entra ID.
  • Each team gets a dedicated SageMaker AI domain that hosts a private SageMaker Studio GUI.
  • Workloads run in separate Kubernetes namespaces, ensuring isolation.
  • HyperPod Task Governance enforces fair resource allocation and compute‑quota management.
  • HyperPod Observability supplies monitoring dashboards for the entire cluster.
  • Storage is split into two tiers:
    • A POSIX‑compliant file system (Amazon FSx for Lustre or OpenZFS) with per‑team shared directories (/fsx/TeamA, /fsx/TeamB) and per‑user home directories (/home/User1, /home/User2).

Component Role

item.title: AWS adds automated remediation workflow using Lambda Durable Functions, EventBridge, and Bedrock
item.description:
AWS adds automated remediation workflow using Lambda Durable Functions, EventBridge, and Bedrock

AWS announced an update that extends the AWS DevOps Agent with an automated remediation workflow built on AWS Lambda Durable Functions, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Bedrock. The new flow keeps the DevOps Agent in its safe observe‑and‑report mode while adding a controlled, programmable step that can apply fixes after a single approval.

🔍 Overview

  • Reducing the time between incident detection, investigation, and remediation is a critical priority for organizations running production workloads on AWS.
  • When an issue arises, on‑call engineers often need to diagnose the problem across components, identify the root cause, and apply a fix, sometimes in the middle of the night.
  • AWS DevOps Agent automatically triages incidents, provides root‑cause analysis (RCA) and recommended actions, but typically does not modify production resources directly.
  • The update demonstrates how to combine AWS Lambda Durable Functions, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Bedrock to automate the remediation step, turning investigation summaries into pre‑validated fixes ready for a single approval.

🧩 How it works

  1. Investigation completed – AWS DevOps Agent emits an event containing symptoms, findings, and RCA.
  2. Event receipt – Amazon EventBridge receives the investigation‑completion event and triggers the devops-agent-trigger Lambda function with the investigation content.
  3. Orchestration start – The trigger function packages the summary and starts the devops-agent-remediation-durable durable function.
  4. Bedrock analysis – The durable function sends the investigation context to Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock analyzes the findings and searches an allowlist of approved Lambda tools (e.g., devops-agent-lambda-tool).
  5. Tool selection – Bedrock proposes specific remediation actions based on the findings and the available tools.
  6. Read‑only execution – For read‑only actions, the durable function runs the selected tools autonomously.
  7. Mutating actions – For infrastructure‑changing actions, the workflow pauses and waits for a human approval signal.
  8. Approval & execution – After approval, the durable function applies the remediation actions using the selected tools.
  9. Iterative loop – The function operates as an agentic loop, repeatedly invoking Bedrock, executing approved tools, and feeding results back until remediation is complete.

⚙️ Key details

  • Lambda Durable Functions can run for up to one year without extra infrastructure, automatically checkpoint progress, suspend during long‑running tasks, and recover from failures.
  • The orchestrator enforces a curated allowlist of remediation tools; each tool is a purpose‑built Lambda function that performs a single, well‑scoped action (e.g., reading a Lambda configuration or updating an IAM policy statement).
  • Read‑only tools run autonomously; mutating tools cause the durable function to pause and wait for an approve/reject signal.
  • The approval signal accepts an arbitrary JSON payload, allowing parameter overrides or reviewer observations to be fed back into the Bedrock conversation before execution.
Tool (allowlist) Purpose
devops-agent-lambda-tool Performs a specific, well‑scoped action such as reading a Lambda configuration or updating an IAM policy statement

🚀 Benefits

  • Reduces mean time to resolution (MTTR) by preparing pre‑validated changes that require only a single approval click.
  • Frees on‑call engineers from repetitive diagnostic and manual remediation steps.
  • Keeps automated actions auditable and safe by limiting execution to an approved set of Lambda tools.
  • Allows the workflow to pause for minutes, hours, or days without consuming compute resources, then resume exactly where it left off.

📈 Real‑world impact – Cornerstone Orion AI

  • Cornerstone OnDemand’s Orion AI, built with Amazon Bedrock and Strands Agents, reduced database incident diagnosis time from 45 minutes to 10 minutes (a 78 % reduction).
  • A three‑person team delivered Orion AI in six months.
  • Orion AI also eliminated a 15‑minute reporting lag between SRE and data teams, reduced redundant alerts by a median of 65 %, and collapsed a four‑step manual handoff into a single interaction.
  • The system illustrates the same principles: AI‑driven investigation, curated tool execution, and human‑in‑the‑loop approval.

The updated workflow shows how AWS services can be combined to automate the full incident‑response loop while preserving control and auditability.

item.title: AWS Adds Voice Travel Concierge to Airline Apps
item.description:
AWS Adds Voice Travel Concierge to Airline Apps

Amazon Web Services has published guidance for adding a voice-operated travel concierge to airline applications, built on three managed services: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Nova Sonic on Bedrock, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The concierge allows travelers to check flights, change seats, and manage bookings through natural spoken requests without leaving the app or navigating screens.

🔍 Overview

Airlines already have apps and websites where travelers check flights, pick seats, and manage bookings. Adding a natural voice layer opens those tasks to spoken requests. With this voice layer, a traveler can change a seat or check a delay by speaking, without leaving the app or navigating through screens. The concierge runs alongside existing screens rather than replacing them, so travelers move between tapping and talking in the same session.

🧩 How It Works

The traveler speaks, and the concierge pulls up their itinerary, changes a seat, updates a meal preference, answers a policy question, and connects them to a live agent on request. The user opens the web application, hosted on AWS Amplify, in a browser or on a mobile device. Amazon Cognito authenticates the request and returns JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) and temporary AWS credentials. The front end opens a SigV4-signed WebSocket connection to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to begin the voice concierge session. The runtime validates the token with Amazon Cognito and initializes Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic through Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic processes the audio and triggers tool calls. The AgentCore Gateway forwards requests as REST API calls to Amazon API Gateway, which routes them to AWS Lambda functions. AWS Lambda functions query Amazon DynamoDB tables for bookings, passengers, seat maps, loyalty status, and flight information.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an agentic platform for building, deploying, and operating AI agents securely at scale with your choice of framework and model. The AgentCore runtime hosts the agent with microVM isolation per session. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend endpoints as discoverable MCP tools.
  • Amazon Nova Sonic on Bedrock is a speech-to-speech model for real-time voice. This implementation uses Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic for real-time speech.
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is a fully managed retrieval augmented generation service that grounds answers in your own documents. It answers policy questions by grounding responses in your airline policy documents.
  • The system streams audio in both directions and holds the thread of a conversation across many turns.
  • The architecture separates the front end, the AI agent, and the backend services into distinct layers, so you can develop and scale each one on its own.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data.
  • The AI layer connects to a sample airline backend with synthetic data, which accelerates your implementation when you adapt the pattern to your own systems.
  • The backend uses AWS Lambda for business logic (itineraries, seat maps, passenger updates, flight status, loyalty, policy lookups, and escalation) and Amazon DynamoDB for data storage (customer profiles, bookings, passengers, seat maps, purchase history, preferences, conversations, and flight data).

🚀 Availability

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Adds Agentic Retrieval to Managed Knowledge Base
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Adds Agentic Retrieval to Managed Knowledge Base

Amazon Bedrock’s Managed Knowledge Base now supports agentic retrieval, an advanced RAG capability that plans and iterates over search steps automatically.

🔍 Overview

  • Agentic retrieval is available on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.
  • Instead of one search, Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base plans the retrieval.
  • It breaks the question into sub‑queries, runs them, judges whether it has enough evidence, and searches again if it doesn’t.
  • Two APIs are provided:
    • Retrieve – runs one hybrid search and returns scored chunks.
    • AgenticRetrieveStream – runs a planning loop and streams the steps back to you as trace events.

🧩 How it works

  • The planner splits the user query into sub‑queries.
  • Each sub‑query is executed against the knowledge base.
  • After each step the system checks whether the accumulated evidence is sufficient.
  • If not, additional sub‑queries are generated and the process repeats.
  • When a passage lacks enough context, a FullDocumentExpansion step calls bedrock:GetDocumentContent to fetch the whole document.

⚙️ Integration with LangChain

  • The langchain-aws package exposes both retrieval modes.
    • The standard Retrieve API appears as a normal LangChain retriever that can be dropped into a chain.
    • The AgenticRetrieveStream API is exposed as a function retrieval directly from a knowledge base.
  • Both paths return document chunks from the knowledge base, which the application then uses to generate a grounded response.

📦 Key Details

  • Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base removes the self‑managed vector store, embeddings, and re‑ranking models from the RAG architecture.
  • You configure a data source (e.g., an Amazon S3 bucket); the service handles chunking, embedding, storage, and retrieval.
  • Boto3 version 1.43.32 or later is required; agentic_retrieve_stream did not exist before that version.
  • The knowledge base assumes a service role with the following permissions:
    • bedrock:GetDocumentContent (often overlooked)
    • s3:ListBucket on the bucket and s3:GetObject on its contents, both conditioned on aws:ResourceAccount
    • If guardrails are used, also bedrock:GetGuardrail and bedrock:ApplyGuardrail
  • A policy with only bedrock:Retrieve works until the planner reaches a whole‑document fetch, then fails.

🚀 Availability & Costs

  • The walkthrough uses the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1).
  • Running the walkthrough may incur costs for document storage, ingestion, retrieval calls, and foundation model inference.
  • Delete the resources when you complete the experiment to avoid ongoing charges.

📊 API Comparison

API Behavior
Retrieve Runs one hybrid search and returns scored chunks.
AgenticRetrieveStream Executes a planning loop, streams each step as trace events, and returns document chunks after iterative retrieval.

item.title: Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege
item.description:
Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege

Amazon Quick now offers a reliable way to downgrade user roles using the AWS Command Line Interface, filling a gap where the console does not support direct transitions such as Admin to Reader or Author to Reader.

🔍 Overview

Managing access permissions effectively is an important aspect of maintaining a secure and collaborative environment. Amazon Quick supports versatile user management options for various identity types. You can provision users natively or through enterprise identity providers like AWS IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Regular audits of user roles are recommended to confirm everyone has appropriate permissions.

🧩 How it works

  • Roles are assigned and grouped according to job functions: Admin, Author, and Reader.
  • The principle of least privilege applies strongly to administration; downgrading roles is a key part of enforcing it.
  • For more granular control, consider Custom Permissions, which restrict capabilities within a role tier.
  • Integration with AWS IAM adds permission boundaries beyond the built-in role system.

⚙️ Key details

  • The console does not provide direct downgrade paths for all transitions (e.g., Admin to Reader or Author to Reader).
  • The update-user API also rejects direct downgrades with a “You cannot downgrade a user role” error.
  • Two reliable solutions exist: manual deletion-and-recreation and a CLI method.
  • The CLI step-down method works for legacy BI-only roles: Admin > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader.
  • The same sequence works for Pro users when intermediate steps use legacy roles (e.g., Author Pro > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader Pro).
  • Before downgrading, verify that users are currently Admin or Author. Downgraded users lose ability to edit resources they previously owned.
  • For large organizations, the CLI method can load user email addresses from a CSV file.
  • AWS CloudShell can be used without specifying the AWS Region, as it uses the current console context.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Quick offers two subscription tiers with distinct role sets:

Subscription Roles Features
Amazon Quick Enterprise Admin Pro, Author Pro, Reader Pro Full BI + AI features (agents, topics, Q&A, stories, generative summaries)
Amazon Quick Sight (BI-only) Admin, Author, Reader Traditional BI authoring and consumption

Prerequisites include an active AWS account with administrator access to Amazon Quick, and the AWS CLI installed and configured if using the CLI method.

💡 Why it matters

  • Role-based pricing means Authors and Admins pay a fixed monthly per-user fee, while Readers use session-based pricing—downgrading can reduce costs.
  • Downgrading helps enforce least privilege, a practice recommended in the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
  • Proactively transferring ownership of dashboards and analyses when responsibilities change prevents orphaned resources and maintains business continuity.

item.title: AWS Cloud Development Kit Enables Infrastructure Definition Using Modern Programming Languages
